bullets: How moving water and wind wear away hard rock at the coast
slides.heading: Erosion: wind and water wear rock away
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow a hard cliff by the sea, and by the end you will be able to explain what erosion is, name what does the wearing, and spot the trap that rocks just crumble by themselves.

bullets: Explain what erosion means: rock being worn away and carried away
Name the movers that do the wearing: waves, currents and wind
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about rocks crumbling on their own.

bullets: Old photos show the same cliff standing further out to sea than it does today
Nobody knocked it down, yet pieces of it have gone - where did they go?
slides.heading: A cliff that gets smaller
slides.notes: Show the two photos and ask: the cliff is smaller, but nobody dug it away. Where did the missing rock go? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because by the end of the lesson you will be able to trace the missing rock.

bullets: Erosion is the wearing away of rock by moving water and wind
Waves hit the cliff, currents carry loose bits along, and wind wears at exposed rock
slides.heading: Erosion wears rock away
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: rock does not vanish by itself - something moving has to wear it, loosen it and carry the bits away.

bullets: A cliff of hard rock stands against the sea
All day, the waves rush at the cliff face
slides.heading: A hard cliff stands by the sea
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the wave rush in at the cliff. On its own the hard rock just stands there - nothing happens until the moving water arrives.

bullets: Wave after wave batters the cliff and cracks the rock
A loose bit breaks off, and the current carries it away
slides.heading: The waves loosen bits of rock
slides.notes: Follow the crack as it appears, then watch the loose bit break off and wash along with the current. The waves did the loosening and the moving water does the carrying.

bullets: Moving water and wind do the wearing, not the rock itself
Wind wears at the rock and helps carry worn-off bits away
slides.heading: Moving water and wind do the wearing
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: on a calm day nothing happens to the cliff. It is the moving water and the wind that do the work, every time.

bullets: Step 1: waves batter the cliff and loosen a chip of rock
Step 2: the current and the wind carry the chip away, so the cliff gets smaller
slides.heading: Worked example: from cliff to pebble
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each mover as you write it; say: notice there is always a mover - water or wind - doing each part of the wearing and carrying.

bullets: Look at a worn pebble on the beach and explain, step by step, how it was worn away from the cliff
Careful - a classmate claims: Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing. Explain to them why that is wrong, and name what really did the wearing
slides.heading: Your turn: who did the wearing?
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing. The fix is that moving water and wind did the wearing, loosening and carrying the bits away.

bullets: On your own: explain what erosion is and name what wears the rock away
Watch out for the trap one last time: Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing. Say what really does the wearing
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - Rocks crumble on their own, with nothing doing the wearing. - and the fix: moving water and wind do the wearing. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still thinks the rock crumbled by itself.

subject: geography
title: Erosion: wind and water wear rock away
